["When evaluating a chest radiograph for suspected congenital lung anomalies, check for the triad of unilateral volume loss, ipsilateral mediastinal shift, and compensatory hyperaeration of adjacent lobes. Specifically, look for vascular anomalies such as a 'kinked' vessel in the cardiophrenic angle, which may indicate pulmonary hypoplasia or agenesis rather than simple atelectasis. This check applies when differentiating between acquired collapse (atelectasis) and developmental defects (hypoplasia/agenesis). Available tools are insufficient if they provide only binary 'normal/abnormal' classifications without anatomical localization or if automated reports fail to identify subtle vascular contours and lobar volume discrepancies, requiring direct visual inspection of the original image.", "When reviewing a chest radiograph for interstitial lung disease, systematically assess the relationship between parenchymal opacities and lung volumes. Check for diffuse interstitial changes (reticular or nodular patterns) and determine if lung volumes are reduced (restrictive pattern) or increased/normal. This check applies when evaluating patients with dyspnea and suspected restrictive physiology to differentiate fibrotic processes from obstructive diseases. Available tools are insufficient when automated classifiers provide uncalibrated opacity scores without volumetric context, or when report generators produce static descriptions that contradict visual evidence of volume loss; in these cases, rely on direct visual inspection of diaphragm position, rib spacing, and mediastinal structures rather than tool outputs."]
